title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: five hours, five silent letters

questions.prompt: A doctor warns that sitting at a computer for five hours does have side-effects. A listener objects: the school's printed day holds three classes only - half past nine, eleven, one o'clock - and three hours is not five. That same day opens at nine, when the pupils log on, and closes at two. Where has the listener gone wrong?

options.text: nine until two is five hours, and that is what the doctor counts
the three classes come to five hours once the pauses are counted in
the grid holds five hours of classes and one hour of pauses
the doctor is counting the hours of a week, not of a day

questions.explanation: Both figures are right, and they count different things. Nothing is wrong with the objection's own arithmetic: three classes are three classes, and the listener counts them correctly. But the doctor is not counting lessons. He is counting time spent sitting at a computer, and the hours a grid leaves between its classes are spent in the same chair as the classes themselves, because the screen is where this school is: there is nowhere else to go at half past ten. Nine until two is five hours, and it is the school's own printed day that gives them. Nor is anything here a weekly total, nor a day made of five teaching hours: the grid puts three classes inside a five-hour stretch, and the gap is the point.

questions.prompt: In a role play, one student has just argued that a virtual school leaves a bullied child alone in a chair for five hours. His partner must hand him something first, then set an objection of his own against it. Tick EVERY reply that does both.

options.text: I think a child works better where nobody stares at him.
I'm afraid I don't agree: the whole class is there on the screen.
I see what you mean, but the bullying stops the day he logs on.
You are making a good point, however I still think you are wrong.
What you say is true, but his panic attacks have stopped.

questions.explanation: Two things have to be true at once, and that is what makes the sorting hard: the reply must hand the other speaker something, and it must then put a reason of its own in the way. Seeing what he means costs nothing and buys a hearing, and the bullying that stops on the morning the child logs on is a reason, not a mood. Admitting that what he says is true and setting the end of the panic attacks against it does the same work, and does it handsomely. The rest fail on one half or the other. Calling the point a good one grants generously - and then adds nothing but the news that the speaker disagrees, which is where the debate started, not where it is answered. Opening on an opinion grants nothing at all, however good the reason that follows. And a polite refusal is still a refusal: the I'm afraid softens the voice, but not one word of the other case is kept.

questions.prompt: Five words are printed in this order: plumber, half, biscuits, autumn, listen. Each of them holds one letter that is written and never sounded. Take those five silent letters, in the order of the words, and they spell a word. Which word do they spell?

options.text: blunt
burnt
burst
brunt

questions.explanation: Say each word aloud before you decide, and do not answer from memory: this is not the chain your book prints. A plumber comes to mend your pipes and there is no b in the sound of him. Half is said as though the l had been rubbed out. Biscuits are said as though the u were not there at all. Autumn ends on the m, and its n waits in the spelling for the day somebody says autumnal. And nobody has ever sounded the t of listen. Written downwards, those five give b, l, u, n, t - blunt, which is what a knife that will not cut is. The word your book builds, burnt, comes from a chain with two other words in it: change one word in the list and the word at the bottom changes with it. That is also the proof that every letter was correctly picked - mistake a single one and no word comes out at all.

questions.prompt: A report follows two pupils. Zack, twelve, enrolled after panic attacks and bullying; Natalie, thirteen, because she was afraid of speaking in class and found her teacher strict. A visitor concludes that both had found the lessons too difficult. What is wrong with his conclusion?

options.text: not one of the two reasons names a lesson; both name its surroundings
one reason names a teacher, so at least one of them is about the lessons
both reasons name other pupils, so both are about the playground
both reasons name fear, so both are about the examinations

questions.explanation: Read the two reasons for what they contain, not for what they suggest. Not one subject is named, no mark is mentioned, no paper has been failed. A rush of fear that seizes the body, three boys in a corridor, the dread of hearing your own voice in a room, an adult whose severity fills the class: all of that surrounds the teaching without ever entering it. The mention of a teacher is tempting, but it is the manner of the person and not the difficulty of what she teaches. Other pupils explain one of the two cases and not the other, since a strict teacher is nobody's classmate. And fear here has no examination anywhere near it - it comes before the lesson begins, not at the end of the year.

questions.prompt: Somebody has just claimed that Mary never went near a virtual school. A pupil wants to answer that she really did put her name on the roll of one, last summer, and to say it with the emphatic form. Which sentence does that?

options.text: Mary did enrol in a virtual school last summer.
Mary did enrolled in a virtual school last summer.
Mary does enrol in a virtual school last summer.
Mary did enrol in a virtual school every summer.

questions.explanation: Two things have to come out right at once here, and only one sentence manages both. As soon as the auxiliary is put into the past, the past leaves the verb: keeping the ending on enrolled makes two words carry the same tense, and the sentence collapses. Choosing the present auxiliary is a second way of getting the tense wrong, this time against the words last summer standing at the end of the line. The dangerous trap is the one whose English is faultless: it is built exactly as it should be, and it says something else - a summer that comes round again and again, which nobody has claimed and which would not answer the doubt raised.

questions.prompt: A pupil says this sentence aloud, pressing her voice on one word only, the word enrolled: "Mary enrolled in a virtual school last summer." Which question has she just answered?

options.text: What did Mary do last summer?
Who enrolled in a virtual school last summer?
What did Mary enrol in?
When did Mary enrol in a virtual school?

questions.explanation: The stressed word is the news, and everything else in the sentence was already in the question. So work backwards: strip out the pressed word and whatever is left has to be what the questioner already knew. Take away the verb and you are left with Mary, a virtual school and last summer - a question that names the person, the place and the moment and asks only what she did. Had the name been pressed instead, the question would have been about which person. Had the school been pressed, the question would have been about what she joined. Had the summer been pressed, the question would have been about the moment. Same words, same order, four different questions answered.
